header:
Date: 2026-12-08 | Start: 15:30 UTC | Duration: 58m | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood Solutions Eng); Sanjay Rao (BrightWave Head of Platform), Evelyn Cho (BrightWave SRE), Marcus Reed (BrightWave ML Eng), Tina Alvarez (BrightWave Procurement)
summary: POC scoping focused on benchmark harness integration and traffic-slicing. Customer wants to run their existing client scripts against Redwood Dedicated and a hosted fallback to compare streaming vs non-streaming token costs and tail latency. Key goals: define success criteria (p99 latency < 300ms for short prompts, 95% throughput for steady-state mix), identify script adapter gaps, finalize timeline for a 2-week benchmark pilot, and confirm data handling (no PII persisted).
topics: Customer scripts and harness adapter requirements
Streaming vs non-streaming throughput and cost tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone thanks for joining on short notice, appreciate it. We're going to run through scope for the POC harness handshake.
[00:14] Sanjay Rao: Thanks Maya, yeah we wanna make sure we can reproduce our production traffic, it's the main blocker for approvals.
[00:28] Daniel Kim: quick intro — I'm Daniel, I'll be helping with the harness adapter and the live run. we usually ask for two things from customers: representative prompt sets and a small client driver (script) that simulates their traffic.
[00:44] Marcus Reed: right yeah we already have a driver — it's in python, uses aiohttp and streams partial tokens. it's been tuned to mimic our UI latency expectations.
[00:58] Evelyn Cho: just to be explicit, we have two traffic slices: short queries (~12 tokens output, 90% of traffic) and long generation (~500 tokens, 10%). burstiness is up to 300 qps for short, sustained 50 qps for long.
[01:15] Maya Patel: perfect. for the POC we typically define three slices: ramp, steady-state, and spike. we'll wire that into the harness. what are your success criteria?
[01:30] Sanjay Rao: primary is p99 tail latency for short queries under 300ms when on dedicated. secondary is 95% of target throughput with <1.5x cost factor compared to our internal inference baseline. also we need telemetry to show KV cache hit-rate and token-level cost.
[01:48] Priya Shah: just to clarify, when you say 'KV cache' you mean prefix cache/kv for chat contexts? sometimes the customers call it key-value cache or K-V cache, so want to make sure matching terms.
[02:02] Marcus Reed: yeah it's the chat KV cache — important cause we rely on prefix reuse. otherwise cost goes up massively.
[02:13] Daniel Kim: noted. our runtime supports automatic prefix caching and we can report cache hit ratios. one caveat: streaming vs non streaming behavior changes batching and therefore tail. for streaming we keep smaller batch windows, so p99 tends to be lower but throughput can dip if clients are chatty.
[02:32] Evelyn Cho: that's exactly the tradeoff we want to quantify. our UI relies on early partial tokens for perceived latency. if streaming kills throughput at scale, we need fallback plan.
[02:45] Maya Patel: ok we'll plan two benchmark passes: pass A = streaming enabled (client-side partials); pass B = non-streaming (full output flush). for both we'll mirror the exact script you run in production.
[03:00] Sanjay Rao: on security — we need to confirm that no customer prompt data is persisted in logs beyond ephemeral telemetry. SOC2 controls are required for procurement.
[03:12] Maya Patel: absolutely. Redwood Dedicated offers optional customer-managed KMS for keying and data at rest. for hosted we'll redact prompts in stored analytics and provide audit logs. we'll attach our SOC2 + ISO docs.
[03:26] Tina Alvarez: we'll need the security pack before legal signs off, plus an explicit data flow diagram.
[03:34] Priya Shah: I can put together a one-page data flow and pointer to audit log retention; will include KMS mappings.
[03:42] Daniel Kim: back to the harness — Marcus, can you describe the driver handshake? do you call an SDK or hit REST endpoints? any custom retry logic?
[03:54] Marcus Reed: our driver wraps our frontend client code, it hits our API gateway which in turn calls the model endpoints. For the POC we can provide a simplified version that calls Redwood directly (we already have API keys in a sandbox). the driver currently streams with SSE; we can switch to chunked streaming if needed.
[04:14] Daniel Kim: perfect. we typically provide a small adapter — a PR to your repo — that standardizes response parsing and metrics emission. we'll plumb in our telemetry hooks so we can correlate request IDs to trace logs.
[04:29] Sanjay Rao: how invasive is that adapter? we want to avoid big changes to our release schedule.
[04:36] Daniel Kim: it's non-invasive — usually a 4-8 file change and a README. for your python driver it should be a 2-3 hour integration for your engineers. Priya will help with the first pass.
[04:49] Priya Shah: yep I'll draft the adapter template and a checklist.
[04:54] Marcus Reed: ok, timeline wise — we want the POC to run for two weeks with a 72-hour steady-state window for analysis. is that normal?
[05:04] Maya Patel: two weeks is a good length. typical plan: week 0 — set up credentials and adapter; week 1 — baseline passes and streaming vs non-streaming runs; week 2 — focused spike tests, cold starts, and final analysis. we can compress if you want but prefer quality.
[05:21] Evelyn Cho: can we also test model variants / quantization config? we might try a float16 vs 8bit quant variant to see cost-latency tradeoffs.
[05:32] Daniel Kim: yes, we can schedule model variant runs. note that quantized paths sometimes change output distribution; we'll include evals on a small pass to check quality regression.
[05:44] Sanjay Rao: about metrics — we'll need per-route token cost, per-token latency breakdown, p50/p95/p99, and cold start percentiles. also, can Redwood expose per-request debug traces? we need those for our SRE analysis.
[05:58] Maya Patel: yes we have per-request traces and token-level billing logs. for Dedicated we can extend retention. I'll include sample dashboards.
[06:08] Tina Alvarez: legal question — if we run with production-like prompts, can Redwood guarantee non-persistence and a right-to-delete?
[06:18] Maya Patel: we can provide contractual language; for Hosted we do pseudonymization in stored analytics and for Dedicated you control retention. we'll loop in legal.
[06:28] Marcus Reed: one more technical item — our UI needs early tokens under 120ms perceived. p99 is fine for overall but perceived latency matters. can the harness capture first-byte times as well as final token?
[06:42] Daniel Kim: yes, we'll emit first-byte and last-byte timestamps in traces, and correlate with client-side RUM if you want.
[06:50] Priya Shah: small gotcha — some of our prompts have long system preamble, so effective sequence length is higher. we'll need to include that in the workload model.
[06:59] Maya Patel: please include those preambles in the prompt samples you send. it's important for kernel selection and batch sizing.
[07:08] Sanjay Rao: can you share an example harness workload file so we can map our slices?
[07:14] Daniel Kim: I'll share the harness workload template and a sample JSON that defines ramp/steady/spike. Expect that in the adapter PR.
[07:22] Sanjay Rao: what about cost modeling? our finance team wants an estimate for 50k monthly active users, which roughly maps to 150 million tokens per month.
[07:34] Maya Patel: we'll run the benchmark numbers and produce a tokenized cost projection with streaming vs non-streaming and with/without caching. include quant variants too.
[07:44] Evelyn Cho: for the spike tests — do you support shaping exact arrival patterns? e.g., Poisson vs fixed inter-arrival?
[07:53] Daniel Kim: yes, the harness supports multiple arrival distributions; we'll match your telemetry histogram if you provide it.
[08:00] Marcus Reed: anything else on infra — we run in multi-region and want fallbacks. does Redwood route and fallback automatically?
[08:09] Maya Patel: yes we can route by region and automatic fallback to a compatible model variant or region when capacity constrained. for Dedicated you can pin region and we can enable cross-region fallback for resilience.
[08:20] Sanjay Rao: ok good. procurement — what do we need to sign to start the POC?
[08:26] Tina Alvarez: procurement will need an MSA addendum for a trial environment and an NDA; also a temporary order for dedicated capacity billed monthly.
[08:36] Maya Patel: we can draft a POC addendum and a temporary capacity order. I'll send a template.
[08:43] Priya Shah: action items recap: Daniel - adapter PR & workload template; Maya - pricing bands, POC addendum, SOC2 pack; Marcus - prompt samples and histograms.
[08:53] Sanjay Rao: sounds good. can we lock a dry run for next Tue (2026-12-15) morning PST?
[09:01] Maya Patel: yes I have availability 09:00-11:00 PST, I'll propose a 45m dry run and a follow-up deep-dive.
[09:10] Evelyn Cho: one last note — we may need a test VPC peering for Dedicated; is that possible for the trial?
[09:18] Daniel Kim: we can do VPC peering for Dedicated trials; there is some networking lead time (1-3 business days). we'll include the networking checklist.
[09:26] Tina Alvarez: procurement will expect an invoice for trial capacity if we go dedicated, please cc billing.
[09:33] Maya Patel: will do. any outstanding questions?
[09:36] Marcus Reed: none from me. thanks.
[09:38] Maya Patel: great — thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the PR and docs.
[09:43] Sanjay Rao: thanks. bye.

Notes and imperfections: occasional transcription swapped 'Run:AI' as 'run AI' in notes, 'K-V cache' appears, some speaker attributions may be slightly off — e.g., a couple lines where Marcus is tagged as 'Speaker 2' in the raw export but corrected above. Links shared: adapter PR template: https://redwood.example.com/poc-adapter-template, SOC2 pack: https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2-pack, harness workload sample: https://redwood.example.com/harness/workload-sample.json
